You come to the fundamental problem of security - you have to trust SOMEBODY otherwise you'd better throw the computer in question into the furnace.

The reasons for still using Windows are myriad. Specialized software, performance/utility when using Windows software, format compatibility pertaining to the aforementioned software, lack of time/ability to retrain yourself/employees/etc., incompatible devices, familiarity, stubbornness, ease of installing software (which, despite the great leaps Linux has made in the last 15 years, can still be a nightmare even in Ubuntu), and a variety of other things. You can probably think of more than a few. In many cases, it comes down to flat-out being able to use the computer. Most people do not have the time, inclination, or fortitude to learn an OS that is fundamentally highly different from what they are used to. While Ubuntu and friends have done a great deal for usability, and grandma may use Ubuntu for her Firefox and word processing, a lot of people need to do a lot more than grandma with their computers, and in many cases, while Windows is suboptimal, it's good enough and they don't have to learn to, say, write a shell script for it, or learn skills they will only rarely find a use for on another computer. What is simple for those inclined towards computers is like trying to learn a foreign language to a lot of other people - obtuse, difficult, nonsensical, requires thinking in entirely different and sometimes painful paradigms, and altogether is usually a lot more trouble than it's worth to get a hamfisted half-hearted knowledge.

However, are these reasons enough? That's a question you'll have to ask yourself.

In terms of trust, however, that is another story entirely. Going back to my opening statement, you have to trust SOMEBODY. That means you have to trust the thousands upon thousands of people who write the hundreds of software packages that are involved in Linux simply booting up, and then the hundreds or thousands involved in doing anything with it. Despite being open source, security audits are quite obviously NOT being continuously run, considering there have been bugs upwards of 40 years old found in some OSS code (and even if they are, these bugs can be extremely subtle). You also have to be certain the bugs aren't "bugs" that are slipped in by someone or other within all that software. Am I saying Linux isn't trustworthy? In truth, I am, but it's more trustworthy than Windows; nevertheless, it's far from perfect. Truth be told, NO software is 100% trustworthy, unless you're able to perfectly audit or prove correct every line of code in any program in the chain used to make or analyze that program, which means you'll probably be analyzing FORTRAN and COBOL from the 60's, assuming it even exists anymore. Realistically speaking, though, Linux is probably better than Windows, by a significant margin, but if you're looking for perfectly trustworthy, it just isn't going to happen. Even your own code may have flaws in it, if you wrote it from the ground up.

Windows 7, of course, is closed source, which makes auditing much, MUCH more difficult, especially since it is (or was) a moving target. Nevertheless, it does have a few things going for it, including the fact that nobody has apparently found anything too terrible over any packet sniffers. Furthermore, if it was continuously uploading tons of data in an unauthorized manner, chances are it would end up being considerably more noticable in terms of raw bandwidth it has consumed. Even if it was all encrypted, this would make it much more difficult. Speculation abounds as to whether or not there are back doors in Microsoft products, but "can get in" is different than "will get in." In the case of Windows 10, the back door question is removed because the system hands Microsoft whatever data it wants on a silver platter - and ultimately that's what it gets, because a patch in the OS can give them access to every scrap of data on there, and the EULA can be twisted in any which way they deem fit, unless you are essentially blackmailed into accepting a EULA change they stick on a patch, since your computer will make a dandy brick if you don't accept it and have Win10 on the computer and no alternatives.

So, let's say that "Windows 7 SP1" is "good enough" in terms of trust. Perhaps not for you, but for others. So what can we do if Microsoft is diddling with the insides?

Simple.

Turn off updates.

This is sacrelig for a lot of people, who believe the second that you do your computer will be part of four Russian botnets and be used as a proxy by some other country's intelligence service for cyberterrorist activities. These people tend to ignore the many downsides of auto-patches. Such as computers that stop working, cough up drivers, and otherwise make life miserable. There's a reason there is (or was) a rollback function, after all. In general, however, there are a few things you can do to mitigate the risk. Virtual machines, sandboxing, and good security software, among others. Of course, can you trust THESE? Maybe. Maybe not. IMO some security software (specifically anti-virus and anti-malware) are NOT trustworthy as some automatically upload things to the anti-virus maker without your permission and give you no way to disable this functionality. But all things considered, they tend to take a very different strategy from patching, and IMO, overall, they tend to work better.

This all sidesteps the question of whether or not the update is on your computer, though. The answer is, at least according to everything I am aware of, that NO, they are NOT, unless you volunteered for Microsoft's customer experience improvement program, or whatever they call it. In that case, yes, if you auto-update and have that enabled, those patches are on your Windows 7 system and it has spyware similar to Windows 10. HOWEVER, it is always possible Microsoft may slip that patch into later updates for the system overall, so ultimately automatic update comes with an increasing number of disadvantages, which include the Windows 10 harassment.

Backing up to the overall question, though - ultimately the decision is yours and yours alone, and specific to your situation. There's little I can do to assess it. Ultimately there are no really good choices in this situation, except MAYBE Android if it matures and gets good Windows compatibility (which may or may not happen), although the fact that half of this stuff is likely in response to Windows starting to collapse in general may make it somewhat irrelevant after a few years.

So my short answer is, "Windows 7, SP 1, unpatched, is reasonably safe from Microsoft's spying, but you need security software and preferably VMs, and Linux is ultimately safer. But there are many reasons to continue to use Windows for many users, even if this isn't a good thing."
